The Adaptive Convexity Framework

Part 3 of 6 · ≈ 13 min read · In pictures · 7 exhibits →

Bitcoin: Convexity Backbone

The Reserve Asset

Bitcoin as the convexity backbone.

Bitcoin is the framework’s reserve asset and its main source of , and much of the rest of the portfolio is arranged around it. The case for holding it rests on properties you can check: a fixed supply schedule, several independent valuation models, and an adoption curve that has so far delivered lopsided gains, well beyond the single-digit compounding of mature assets.

You can hold Bitcoin under your own keys or through regulated funds (spot ETFs), and you can pledge it as collateral for a loan. It is also violently volatile, which the framework handles with sizing instead of treating it as a reason to stay out. Its inclusion is doctrine. Its accumulation pace follows valuation discipline, with its informing conviction; both are written guidance you apply. It is scored like every other holding, but the score neither sizes nor sells it. Bitcoin sits outside the three postures and the concentration limits, and this part’s rules govern it. As of September 2026 the dashboard shows Bitcoin’s CIS (Part 6 explains the score) and can overlay the power-law trend and floor on its price chart; nothing in the software paces purchases.

Handling Doctrine · Accumulate

  • Accumulate only. Bitcoin is never sold, traded, or rebalanced.
  • Models inform pacing, not execution. Valuation models shape conviction and how fast you buy; they never call an entry or an exit.
  • Liquidity comes from elsewhere. Income and non-Bitcoin assets supply cash, leaving the reserve intact.

Handling Doctrine · Borrow

  • Collateral, not sale. Liquidity is accessed via Bitcoin-backed borrowing rather than liquidation.
  • Optional, and only at scale. Borrowing becomes an option once the reserve is large relative to any loan, and every loan stays inside the loan-to-value rules below.
  • Borrow for cash flow. Loans fund income-producing assets whose cash flow pays the interest, never living costs. The core is not sold to fund spending, though a lender can sell pledged coins if a loan hits its trigger or a payment is missed, and that sale is a taxable event.

Structural Fit

Why Bitcoin specifically.

Naming an asset the backbone invites one challenge above all others: why this one, and not gold, stocks or real estate? The framework’s objective is the most compounding a person can survive over decades of regime instability, and the backbone is judged against ten requirements drawn from that objective. The fair suspicion about any list like this is that someone wrote it backward from the answer. The defense is that each item follows from the objective, and you can check them one at a time. If another asset met all ten at once, it would qualify equally. The ten are:

  1. Dual custody

    holdable both under your own keys and through regulated funds, with the same underlying exposure and little basis risk. Both routes must exist; the reserve does not have to use both.

  2. Collateralization

    a lending market deep enough to borrow against the asset instead of selling it.

  3. Convexity (order-of-magnitude upside)

    an addressable market many times the asset’s current value (the estimate later in this part is about 13 times Bitcoin’s start-of-2026 market cap), far beyond the two- or threefold growth of a mature asset.

  4. Regime resilience

    has survived every regime shock so far and gone on to new highs after each completed cycle (a judgment about the future, not a guarantee).

  5. Quantifiable models

    several independent valuation models that anyone can recompute.

  6. Single asset

    one fungible asset, the same everywhere. Every building, by contrast, is a different building.

  7. Tax efficiency

    can be held for decades without a forced sale, borrowed against, and passed to heirs with a stepped-up basis under current US law, leaving tax-advantaged space for Torque that may rotate.

  8. Multi-decade survivability

    a high probability of still existing, and still working, 30 to 60 years from now.

  9. Passive hold-ability

    nothing to manage, roll over or maintain once it is set up. Self-custody still needs a key backup and an inheritance plan; the risk register below covers what happens without them.

  10. Instant liquidity

    you can add to it in minutes and borrow against it in days, where property takes months.

Gold is the closest alternative at 7.5 out of 10. It satisfies collateralization, single-asset focus, tax efficiency, passive holding, multi-decade survivability and liquidity, and earns partial credit on custody (physical metal carries dealer premiums and storage costs a fund share does not), on models and on regime resilience. What it offers is preservation of purchasing power; it has no order-of-magnitude upside. The S&P 500 follows at 6, and real estate and commodities trail, short mainly on convexity and custody. None of the four clears all ten. The ranking follows from the framework’s own objectives (surviving many cycles, capturing convexity tax-efficiently and keeping your options open), and a different objective could be served by a different asset.

Why Not 100% Bitcoin

Optimizing for multi-cycle survivability.

If Bitcoin clears every requirement, a sharper question follows: why hold anything else? Plenty of holders argue exactly that. If you never sell, why not go 100 percent Bitcoin? In a long bull market the all-in holder wins in raw dollars, and the framework does not pretend otherwise: someone with 100 percent in Bitcoin through a tenfold rise ends with far more than someone with 15 percent. The framework accepts that trade. It aims at a different target, the best outcome weighted by probability across several cycles, for a real person who will meet job losses, health scares, family needs and a regime shift or two over three or four Bitcoin cycles.

, the lasting damage a large drawdown does to compounding when it arrives at the wrong moment, grows when one asset makes up most of the portfolio. A concentrated holder has little else to sell, or to spend at a multi-year low, so volatility can only be endured. Income-funded is the usual answer, but the paycheck that funds it can shrink or stop in the same downturn that sinks Bitcoin, because job losses rise in exactly the kind of stress that hits risk assets.

Concentrated systems depend on favorable sequencing. Structured systems are designed for adverse sequencing.

An illustration on actual Bitcoin prices, with simplified sleeves: two investors start with $100,000 in January 2021 and hold their convictions through December 2025. A keeps buying Bitcoin from income; B follows the framework’s rules.

Investor A · 100% Bitcoin

2.86 BTC at $35,000. Before any DCA, the position peaks at ~$197,000 (Nov 2021, Bitcoin ~$69,000) and troughs at ~$44,000 (Nov 2022, Bitcoin ~$15,500), a 77% drawdown. With DCA it reaches about $410,000 at the October 2025 high (Bitcoin ~$126,000) and ends 2025 at ~3.26 BTC, worth ~$285,000 at the year-end close of ~$87,500. A captured every dollar of upside and never had anything else to sell or deploy.

Investor B · Framework

$15K Bitcoin, $40K regime equities, $30K income, $15K dry powder. The 77% BTC drawdown costs ~$23,000, under a quarter of the starting portfolio. At the trough B steps up its Bitcoin buying and spends on AI and growth stocks that fell by half or more in 2022. B ends 2025 with about 0.90 BTC (~$79,000) and about $100,000 across its other sleeves, rebuilt dry powder included: ~$179,000 in all, with Bitcoin at 44% of net worth.

A finished about $106,000 ahead, as it should: when the path cooperates, maximum exposure earns the biggest raw return. Treat B’s figures as a simplified illustration. Its other sleeves are carried at a round $100,000 instead of being modeled holding by holding, and nothing here is a backtest. B’s 44 percent Bitcoin share is also what one strong cycle happened to produce, above the 20–30 percent elevated range set out at the end of this part; it is an outcome, and nobody should read it as a target.

The real difference is what each investor maximized. A maximized exposure; B maximized control. At the 2022 trough B had cash to deploy and income that did not depend on selling Bitcoin, and A had neither. Maximum exposure wins in ideal conditions. Structured architecture wins across uncertain conditions. The second of those sentences is the framework’s design claim, and one cycle cannot prove it; this example shows what control costs in a strong cycle. The advantage the framework claims comes from structure instead of forecasting: cash inside the portfolio, exposure to more than one regime, rules for when to buy, and income that does not depend on Bitcoin.

Discipline, Not Timing

Accumulate, don’t trade.

If control comes from how a position is built, then the way the reserve is assembled matters more than the price of any single purchase. The framework treats Bitcoin as a reserve you accumulate over years. Purchases are systematic and paid from income, and the reserve is held through whole cycles instead of being moved in and out.

The arithmetic rewards patience. A fixed contribution buys a variable number of units (units received equal dollars divided by price), so a lower price buys more of them. The volatility that punishes a trader trying to time an exit works for the steady accumulator, who collects the most units exactly when conviction is hardest to hold.

Valuation discipline, developed under Valuation Models below, sets the pace. When the independent models agree that price is more than 30 percent below their combined estimate, you raise contributions by about half or deploy dry powder. When price runs well above them, you slow discretionary buying and bank income as dry powder, while the systematic income-funded purchases continue. Neither case ever calls for selling the core reserve. Selling would bring back the three failures the design exists to avoid: from a mistimed exit, a tax bill on a realized gain, and the behavioral error of selling into weakness. An accumulator never has to pick an exit, so none of the three ever comes up.

This is the Accumulate phase of a longer lifecycle. Once the reserve has grown into a large share of net worth, borrowing against it becomes an option: the Borrow phase, covered at the end of this part. The refusal to trade is what keeps that option open, because a position never sold is still there to borrow against, or to pass to heirs with a stepped-up basis under current law. All of it assumes the asset itself survives, which is what the risk register examines next.

Risk Register

What can break.

Whether the asset endures is partly a question of plumbing, and in 2024 and 2025 the plumbing changed. US regulators approved spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024, opening allocation through regulated funds; institutions that had publicly dismissed the asset began serving client demand for it; and the policy debate moved from whether Bitcoin is legitimate to how it should be held. For the framework, that cycle tested the rails this part depends on (regulated funds, institutional custody and lending against coins) at scale for the first time. One cycle cannot prove permanence. Volatility did not go away, the long-term path is still uncertain, and better access does not shorten the list below.

Maturity lowers these risks without removing them. The reserve ranges set out below (a 10 to 15 percent target, 20 to 30 percent at higher conviction) are sized for both the upside and the ways it can go wrong.

Protocol & technical

Undiscovered cryptographic flaws, consensus failures, or quantum computers strong enough to break the signatures that protect coins.

Custody loss

Lost private keys, a failed inheritance plan, compromised hardware, or a multisig arrangement whose signers can no longer coordinate, any of which can lock the owner out for good.

Regulatory & tax

Bans, confiscatory taxation, identity rules (KYC) that make some coins worth less than others, or ETF delistings that force a sale.

ETF risk

For anyone holding Bitcoin through ETFs: counterparty failures, fund closures, tracking error, or changes to how ETFs are taxed in qualified accounts.

Market structure gaps

Liquidity that vanishes in a crisis, exchange failures, or stablecoin collapses that cut the routes between dollars and Bitcoin.

Leverage cascades

Forced liquidations of leveraged positions that feed on themselves and push price far below anything fundamentals justify. On October 10, 2025, more than $19 billion of leveraged crypto positions was liquidated in about a day, the largest such wipeout on record.

Miner economics shocks

Hash-rate collapses, centralization, or energy-cost spikes that make mining unprofitable and weaken the network’s security.

Geopolitical controls

Coordinated access restrictions, on-ramp closures, or internet-infrastructure disruption.

Lender counterparty risk

A lender or custodian that goes bankrupt (Celsius and BlockFi both did in 2022), re-lends pledged coins, or relies on contract clauses that let it keep them.

Technology displacement

A better monetary technology that makes Bitcoin obsolete despite its network effects.

Most of those are tail risks you guard against and rarely feel. The one every holder feels is volatility. Plan for Bitcoin drawdowns of 75 to 80 percent: every completed cycle through 2022 fell at least 77 percent (2011, 2013 to 2015, 2017 to 2018 and 2021 to 2022), and the 2025–2026 fall reached about 54 percent. At a reserve-sized position, even the worst of those is a survivable toll paid for the upside, and the exhibit below runs the arithmetic.

Valuation Discipline

Why Bitcoin can be modeled.

Sizing keeps the downside survivable. It does not tell you what the reserve is worth. Bitcoin helps here in one unusual way: its supply is fixed by code (21 million coins, with issuance halving roughly every four years), so the models only have to explain demand, which tracks adoption, liquidity and network effects. That makes its growth look more like a technology platform’s than a currency’s. Plotted on log-log axes against days since the genesis block (January 3, 2009), its price since 2010 has clustered around a of the form Price = A × (Days)B, where A and B are fitted constants whose stability is debated. The framework uses it as context for judging where a cycle stands and never as a forecast; the pattern could break if adoption changes course. The corridor below sketches that trendline, with bands above and below, on a representative price path.

No single model is enough on its own, so the framework reads five: four valuation models and one directional reading of liquidity. When they agree, confidence rises; when they pull apart, so does caution.

  1. Power-law bands

    a log-log regression of price against days since the genesis block, published by Giovanni Santostasi (Reddit, 2018); the corridor with support and resistance bands is Harold Christopher Burger’s (“Bitcoin’s natural long-term power-law corridor of growth,” Medium, 2019). Price has swung far above the trend in manias and below the lower band in capitulations. The fit shifts with the data window and method, so read it as multi-year context and never as a precise value.

  2. Realized price (on-chain cost basis)

    Bitcoin’s aggregate on-chain cost basis, with each coin valued at the price it last moved. It has tended to rise from one cycle to the next, though it can fall, since a coin that changes hands below the price it last moved at pulls it down. It marks an important bear-market level and is no hard floor: price traded below it for months at a time in 2018–19 and again in 2022–23.

  3. Adoption & network models

    Metcalfe’s law and S-curve adoption models value the network by its growth instead of its price. Network size is itself an estimate (addresses are not users), so these models confirm multi-year trends and place Bitcoin on its adoption curve; they are no use for timing.

  4. Production cost

    what it costs a miner to produce a coin, which varies widely with machine efficiency and electricity prices. It marks a pressure zone rather than a floor: when price stays below cost, the least efficient miners switch off, and mining difficulty then adjusts down to the survivors’ costs.

  5. Global liquidity (Alden; Callahan)

    a directional reading of Bitcoin against global liquidity (M2, central-bank balance sheets, real rates), and no valuation model. Bitcoin has tended to move in the same direction as global liquidity over multi-month windows: in 83 percent of 12-month periods and 74 percent of 6-month periods from 2013 to mid-2024, and more sensitively than traditional assets over longer time frames, according to “Bitcoin: A Global Liquidity Barometer” (written by Sam Callahan, commissioned and advised by Lyn Alden, September 2024). The study measures direction, not a fixed multiple, and the link weakens over short windows. Expanding liquidity is a tailwind and tight real rates a headwind; neither sets a fair value.

Fair value, in this part, means the estimate the independent models converge on. It is a judgment you form from them, and it is never the power-law trend on its own. Convergence sets conviction and the pace of buying, and Bitcoin is never sold on a model signal. As of September 2026 the dashboard draws two power-law lines on Bitcoin’s price chart, a trend of 2.88 × (days ÷ 1000)5.82 and a floor of 1.2828 × (days ÷ 1000)5.928; it draws no euphoria band and computes no convergence. Its floor is not a hard floor. Closing prices fell below it in 2015, briefly in 2016, in March 2020, from November 2022 to January 2023, from August to October 2023, and for most of February to mid-September 2026. On September 29, 2026, Bitcoin at about $83,600 sat just above the floor (about $82,900) and about 45 percent below the trend (about $152,000).

Models cluster near price

Confidence in your reserve range rises. Maintain your chosen range, keep the systematic DCA running, and make no sharp changes.

Models converge on undervaluation

Price more than 30% below the models’ combined estimate. While the discount lasts, raise DCA about 50% or deploy dry powder. Existing holdings stay untouched.

Models diverge widely

Uncertainty is high, and the disagreement is itself information. Hold your range, make no sharp changes either way, and wait for the models to come back together.

Through Three Cycles

  • Late 2021 · extension. Near $69,000 on November 10, Bitcoin traded at about 3 times the software’s power-law trend and far above its realized price. Framework response: slow discretionary buying and bank income as dry powder while the systematic DCA continues; sell nothing.
  • Late 2022 · convergence on undervaluation. At the November 21 low near $15,500, Bitcoin stood at about 0.42 times the trend and about 20 percent below the software’s floor line, and the models agreed on deep undervaluation. Framework response: accelerate DCA and deploy the dry powder built during the extension; core holdings never sold.
  • 2025–2026 · muted extension, then a long break below the floor. The October 2025 high near $126,000 sat only about 15 percent above the software’s trend line. Price first closed below the software’s floor line in February 2026, spent most of the next seven months under it, bottomed near $58,000 about 24 percent below it at the turn of June and July, and closed back above it on September 21. Framework response: accelerate DCA and deploy the dry powder; core holdings never sold.

Addressable Market & Implementation

TAM, custody, and the borrow phase.

A valuation is only as useful as the scale it is measured against, which brings in the addressable market and then the mechanics of holding. Bitcoin’s market capitalization at the start of 2026 was ~$1.75 trillion (about 19.97 million coins at ~$87,500), roughly 6 percent of gold’s ~$30 trillion above-ground stock (World Gold Council). On September 29, 2026 it was about $1.68 trillion (about 20.1 million coins at about $83,600), still roughly 6 percent. The doctrine’s estimate counts only the share of existing monetary assets Bitcoin could plausibly absorb:

Gold coexistence · ~$12T

Growing to 30–50% of gold’s ~$30 trillion market value over 20 years, with gold’s market largely intact.

Real-estate value storage · ~$3T

Some of the property held mainly to preserve wealth moving to a store of value that is easier to carry and divide.

Offshore wealth · ~$5T

A share of cross-border holdings (about $15.7 trillion at the end of 2025, per BCG), where self-custody offers a different set of intermediaries and custody risks.

EM currency substitution · ~$3T

Savings in economies with inflation above 20%, as payment rails, custody and regulatory clarity develop.

The four pools add up to about $23 trillion of addressable monetary premium, the doctrine’s estimate and about 13 times Bitcoin’s start-of-2026 market cap. It leaves out new uses such as settlement-layer or DeFi applications. By default, when no research profile supplies its own figure, the dashboard scores Bitcoin against a smaller pool, about $11.5 trillion, so the default score does not depend on this estimate; a separate display scenario builds a pool from three sources and divides by the 21 million cap (as of September 2026; the Math page has the formulas).

Now run one scenario on its own. If Bitcoin reaches 40 percent of gold’s market value over 20 years, that is a $12 trillion market cap: about $570,000 a coin across the 21 million cap, or about 6.5 times the start-of-2026 price of about $87,500. In a $100,000 portfolio, a 15 percent allocation ($15,000) would become about $98,000, adding about $83,000, or about 83 percent of the starting portfolio before anything the other 85 percent earns. It is one conditional path, and no forecast.

means holding appreciated assets instead of selling them, borrowing against them for cash, and leaving them to heirs. It is the main reason the reserve lives in a taxable account. Since January 2026 the framework holds Bitcoin outside Roth by default, for three reasons. First, the reserve is never sold, and under current US law (IRC §1014) an asset inherited at death generally takes a basis equal to its value at death, so a taxable holding passed to heirs leaves none of its lifetime gain to tax as income. Second, only a taxable holding can be pledged for a loan; using an IRA as security for a loan counts as a distribution (IRC §408(e)(4)). Third, Roth space is scarce and better spent on Torque that may rotate. None of this is special to Bitcoin. It works for any appreciated capital asset, depends on current law and on credit staying available, and carries interest cost and liquidation risk. Gifts made during life keep the giver’s basis (§1015), and pre-tax retirement accounts get no step-up at all: heirs owe income tax on what they withdraw. What the account choice is worth over decades is worked in Part 4 and in Part 5’s compounding example.

Custody. The framework’s default is the full reserve in self-custody, on hardware wallets, in a taxable account, bought through payroll DCA and never trimmed on valuation. Spot Bitcoin ETFs carry the same exposure through a regulated fund. As of September 2026 the dashboard treats them like native Bitcoin for its concentration and add-limit exemptions, and counts them in the Bitcoin allocation only in an optional mode (native holdings by default). The Borrow phase is optional and depends on scale: it may begin after 15 to 20 years of accumulation, if the reserve has grown into the mature share described below. A loan supplies cash without a sale, but it adds interest cost and the risk of a forced sale: if the collateral falls far enough, or a payment is missed, the lender sells it, and that sale is a taxable event. Pledged coins also leave self-custody for the lender’s custody or a shared multisig for the life of the loan; until a loan is opened, no custodian is involved. The rules below exist to keep that risk survivable.

  1. Conservative loan-to-value. Treat 20–35 percent as an illustrative operating range. A low starting loan-to-value lowers liquidation risk; it does not guarantee surviving any given drawdown. Loan-to-value rises as the collateral falls: LTV after a fall equals starting LTV ÷ (1 − the fall). After a 70 percent fall in Bitcoin, a loan opened at 20 percent stands near 67 percent LTV, one opened at 25 percent near 83, at 30 percent at 100, and at 35 percent near 117, before interest. Lenders commonly issue a margin call near 70 percent LTV, sell collateral if the call is not met, and sell automatically somewhere between 80 and 86 percent (Ledn, Arch, Strike and Coinbase terms, September 2026; each lender sets its own). The fall a loan can absorb before a 70 percent call is 1 − starting LTV ÷ 0.70: about 71 percent from a 20 percent start and 50 percent from 35. Riding out a repeat of the 77 percent drawdown of 2021 to 2022 without a call means opening at about 16 percent or less. The 2025–2026 fall of about 54 percent would have taken a 35 percent loan to about 76 percent LTV, past a typical call. Some lenders allow a start as high as 50 percent; a loan opened there is called after a fall of about 29 percent.

  2. Borrow only for cash-flowing assets. Put borrowed money into income-producing assets whose cash flow pays the interest, never into living costs. Collateral and the asset it funds can fall at the same time; the paydown reserve in rule 3 exists for that case.

  3. Emergency deleveraging plan. Set tripwires that require a paydown if LTV approaches 40–50 percent, and hold liquid reserves large enough to cut principal by 25–50 percent if needed.

  4. Lender diversification & custody verification. Split borrowing across two or three custodians. Before pledging, check that coins are held segregated and bankruptcy-remote, and read the liquidation terms.

  5. Know when not to borrow. Do not open a loan during extreme volatility (VIX above 30, or Bitcoin 30 percent or more below fair value, the models’ convergent estimate) or when the rest of the portfolio is already under stress.

  6. Manage interest-rate risk. Published rates from US Bitcoin-backed lenders ran from about 6 percent (variable) to about 16 percent APR in September 2026; most fixed-rate quotes for retail-sized loans sat near 9 to 12 percent (Ledn: 9.25 to 11.49 percent by loan size), and the cheapest quotes usually require a lower starting LTV or a larger loan. Fix the rate where possible; if it floats, require deployed returns at least three points above the cost.

How large should the reserve be? It scales with horizon and risk capacity. A 10–15 percent target suits horizons of ten years or more and moderate risk capacity. A 20–30 percent elevated range suits higher conviction and longer horizons, and still needs valuation discipline. A 30–50 percent mature share may emerge after 15–20 years through accumulation and appreciation, never by rebalancing up to it, and that is when the Borrow phase becomes an option. These percentages describe outcomes under given conditions, not rebalanced targets. Run the drawdown arithmetic before you pick one: at a fixed weight, a repeat of the 77 percent drawdown of 2021 to 2022 costs about 11.5 percent of the portfolio at a 15 percent reserve and about 7.7 percent at 10 percent. As of September 2026, the dashboard proposes a 15 percent Bitcoin baseline at setup (10 percent under the Conflict Economy and Re-industrialization theses), which you confirm or replace with your own conviction. Its construction score carries a 10 percent Bitcoin posture reference within a 5 to 15 percent band as reference metadata; it costs no points and never triggers a sale. Part 5 builds the rest of the portfolio around the reserve.

Key Insight

The result is lopsided. Before any borrowing, the most the reserve can lose is the reserve itself, a share of net worth set by sizing, while the upside is open-ended and uncertain. A loan changes the first half of that sentence, which is why the borrowing rules are as strict as they are. What the framework adds is everything around the position: the cash, income and rules that let you keep it through full cycles, add to it in dislocations and, if you choose, borrow against it instead of selling.

End of Part 3

Part 3 made the case for Bitcoin as the framework’s reserve asset: accumulated from income, never sold, sized so its drawdowns stay survivable, and paced by valuation models read together. It sits under your own keys in a taxable account, where it can be borrowed against or passed to heirs instead of sold. Borrowing is a late, optional phase with its own loan-to-value rules.
